**CPF Ordinary Wage versus Additional Wage classification by employment month and payable date** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** The stated salary is for employment in March, but is payable on 20 April, after the 14th of the following month. It therefore is not March OW and is classified as AW for that month. AW may still attract CPF, subject to its applicable annual ceiling and contribution rate; the pay-period label alone does not make it OW. [CPF | What constitutes wages for CPF contributions](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/employer/employer-obligations/what-constitutes-wages-for-cpf-contributions)

**Source:** CPF | What constitutes wages for CPF contributions (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF Ordinary Wage versus Additional Wage classification by employment month and payable date): Under the CPF Act, wages are defined as remuneration in money, including any bonus that is due or granted to a person in respect of his employment.

Only payments that are considered wages should be included when declaring wage information and computing CPF contributions.

Payments to include as wages

Basic wage: Salary payable to an employee for work done.
Overtime pay: Payment to an employee for working beyond normal working hours.
Bonus: Payment such as performance bonus.
Allowance: For example, meal allowance and transport allowance.
Commission: For example, sales commission.
Cash incentive: For example, productivity incentive.

Payments not to include as wages

Termination benefit: Compensation that is not given for services or work done by the employee. For example, retrenchment benefit.
Reimbursement: Reimbursement incurred on behalf of the employer for official purposes. The reimbursement amount must not exceed the expenditure incurred. For example, purchase of office stationery.
Benefit in kind: Non-cash benefit or gift given to the employee. For example, a commemorative watch.

Classifying wages as Ordinary Wages or Additional Wages

After determining that a payment is wages, classify it correctly as Ordinary Wages or Additional Wages. The wage type affects how CPF contributions are computed and how the wage information should be declared.

Total Wages is the sum of Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. CPF contributions are computed on the Total Wages payable to an employee in a calendar month, subject to the applicable Ordinary and Additional Wage ceilings.

For wages to be classified as Ordinary Wages for the month, they must meet both of the following conditions:

* They are given to an employee for their employment in that month; and
* They are payable by the 14th of the following month.

For example, monthly salary.

Wages which are not classified as Ordinary Wages will be Additional Wages for the month.

For example, annual performance bonus.

The Additional Wage ceiling sets the maximum amount of AW that attracts CPF contributions in a calendar year for all employees. It is applied on a per employee, per employer, per calendar year basis.

The ceiling is S$102,000 less the employee’s CPF-subject OW for 2026, per employer; an exact CPF-subject bonus amount also needs year-to-date AW and expected full-year OW. - **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF additional wage ceiling based on the contractual due-and-payable year): Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling
The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a
per employer, per year basis. The AW ceiling applies to all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (SPR).
AW ceiling Calculation
The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.
Note: The applicable AW ceiling depends on the due and payable date of the AW. For example, if the 2025 bonus is due and payable to the employee in 2026, then the employer should contribute
according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF newly obtained PR status and OW/AW payable-date treatment): As a Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR), you are required to make CPF contributions on wages earned in Singapore.
CPF contributions are not payable for employees who are neither Singapore Citizens nor SPRs.
Your CPF contribution rates as an SPR depend on how long you have held Permanent Resident status.
First-year rate: Applies from the day you obtain your SPR status, [i.e. the date indicated on your Entry Permit (Form 5/5A) issued by the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA)] until the last day of the month of your first anniversary of SPR.
Second-year rate: Applies from the month following your first anniversary as an SPR until the last day of the month of your second anniversary.
Third-year rate: Applies from the month following your second anniversary as an SPR onwards.
Example
If you have obtained your SPR status on 15 January 2026, the start and end dates for first, second and third year of obtaining SPR status are shown in the table below:

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports CPF newly obtained PR status and OW/AW payable-date treatment): Under the CPF Act, wages are defined as remuneration in money, including any bonus that is due or granted to a person in respect of his employment.

Only payments that are considered wages should be included when declaring wage information and computing CPF contributions.

Payments to include as wages

Basic wage: Salary payable to an employee for work done.
Overtime pay: Payment to an employee for working beyond normal working hours.
Bonus: Payment such as performance bonus.
Allowance: For example, meal allowance and transport allowance.
Commission: For example, sales commission.
Cash incentive: For example, productivity incentive.

Payments not to include as wages

Termination benefit: Compensation that is not given for services or work done by the employee. For example, retrenchment benefit.
Reimbursement: Reimbursement incurred on behalf of the employer for official purposes. The reimbursement amount must not exceed the expenditure incurred. For example, purchase of office stationery.
Benefit in kind: Non-cash benefit or gift given to the employee. For example, a commemorative watch.

Classifying wages as Ordinary Wages or Additional Wages

After determining that a payment is wages, classify it correctly as Ordinary Wages or Additional Wages. The wage type affects how CPF contributions are computed and how the wage information should be declared.

Total Wages is the sum of Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. CPF contributions are computed on the Total Wages payable to an employee in a calendar month, subject to the applicable Ordinary and Additional Wage ceilings.

For wages to be classified as Ordinary Wages for the month, they must meet both of the following conditions:

* They are given to an employee for their employment in that month; and
* They are payable by the 14th of the following month.

For example, monthly salary.

Wages which are not classified as Ordinary Wages will be Additional Wages for the month.

For example, annual performance bonus.

The Additional Wage ceiling sets the maximum amount of AW that attracts CPF contributions in a calendar year for all employees. It is applied on a per employee, per employer, per calendar year basis.

The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a

The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.

according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.
